To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1. Local dense connectivity, where only a few previous layers are connected to each layer, can lead to better accuracy than the standard fully dense connectivity.

(a) dense architectures with local dense connectivity outperform their global dense counterparts on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN, (b) dense architectures with global dense connectivity are more efficient than their non-dense counterparts on the same three datasets, and (c) dense architectures with both local and global dense connectivity outperform both of these baselines on the three datasets.

(i) DenseNets can be made more efficient by allowing for increased growth rates at fixed network capacity, (ii) this is achieved by introducing local dense connectivity, and (iii) local dense connectivity can lead to higher accuracy on image classification benchmarks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (1) To what extent is the full dense connectivity of the original DenseNet architecture necessary?
answering the questions: How can we best reuse features in dense architectures? And, how does the reuse of features impact the accuracy of the model?
the following two questions: (a) What is the optimal number of previous layers to connect to in dense architectures?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proposed local dense connectivity is a promising alternative to the conventional dense connectivity, and it is worth exploring in future work.
DenseNets with less connectivity, allowing more growth rate, achieve better accuracy and are computationally more efficient than DenseNets with full connectivity, allowing less growth rate.
the DenseNet architecture is more efficient than the ResNet architecture.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
DenseNet can be made more efficient by allowing for increased growth rates and reduced depth, while maintaining the same level of performance.
DenseNet can achieve better performance than ResNet by using less parameters.
DenseNets can be made deeper, wider and denser without compromising accuracy, and can be trained in a more efficient manner.
The main takeaway from our work is that
dense connectivity does not have to be global in order to achieve high performance on image classification tasks.
dense architectures are not necessarily more parameter-efficient than their standard CNN counterparts.
DenseNets are robust to changes in connectivity, and thus the choice of connectivity can be made based on the computational resources available, the desired network capacity and the task at hand.
